label: Why Symplectic Topology
notes: Welcome to the opening lecture, drawn from printed pages 1 through 8. Symplectic topology grew out of classical mechanics yet became its own subject once global rigidity phenomena appeared. We preview the form, the flow, and the surprising tension between local flexibility and global obstruction that organizes the whole book.

label: From Mechanics to Geometry
notes: Hamilton rewrote Newtonian motion on phase space, pairing each position with a conjugate momentum. The flow of a single energy function steers every trajectory. Encoding that pairing geometrically gives the symplectic form, and this transition from physics to intrinsic geometry is the historical seed of the entire discipline.

label: The Symplectic Form
notes: On phase space the canonical two-form sums the wedge of each momentum differential with its position differential. Being closed and nondegenerate, it measures signed area in every conjugate plane. Unlike a metric it pairs displacements antisymmetrically, so it records oriented area rather than length, which is the structure we will study throughout.

label: Hamilton's Equations
notes: Given an energy function, the symplectic form converts its differential into a unique vector field whose integral curves are the motions. The equations say position rates equal momentum derivatives of energy and momentum rates equal minus position derivatives. The form is exactly the device translating gradients into dynamics.

label: Flows Preserve Area
notes: Because the Hamiltonian field is defined through the closed form, its flow drags that form to itself, so the form is conserved along motion. Liouville's theorem follows: phase-space volume is invariant. A region may stretch and fold wildly while its total signed area stays fixed, a conservation law with no Newtonian analogue.

label: Darboux: Local Flexibility
notes: Darboux's theorem says every symplectic manifold looks locally like standard phase space; there are no local invariants such as curvature. Moser's deformation argument supplies a slick proof. Locally everything is flexible and identical, so any genuine distinction between symplectic manifolds must be a global, not a pointwise, phenomenon.

label: Local Versus Global
notes: The defining tension of the field is now visible. Locally Darboux flattens all symplectic manifolds to one model, yet globally rigid obstructions appear that no local chart can detect. The course is organized around finding those global invariants that survive once the deceptive local uniformity is stripped away.

label: Gromov Nonsqueezing
notes: Gromov's 1985 theorem is the first hard rigidity result. A symplectic embedding of a ball of radius r into an infinite cylinder forces the cylinder radius to be at least r. Volume would permit squeezing freely, so this is a purely symplectic obstruction, and it births the notion of a capacity.

label: Capacities and Embeddings
notes: A symplectic capacity assigns each region a number that is monotone under embeddings and scales like area. Nonsqueezing makes the cylinder capacity equal to the cross-sectional area. Capacities turn embedding questions into inequalities, and the precise embedding thresholds for ellipsoids and balls remain an active and delicate research frontier.

label: Arnold Conjecture
notes: Arnold predicted that a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism must have at least as many fixed points as a function on the manifold has critical points. This forces far more fixed points than topology alone demands. Proving it drove the creation of Floer homology, a cornerstone of modern symplectic methods.

label: J-Holomorphic Curves
notes: Gromov introduced an auxiliary almost complex structure tamed by the form and studied curves solving a Cauchy-Riemann equation. These J-holomorphic curves are the central technical tool: nonsqueezing, capacities, and the Arnold conjecture all rest on counting them. They convert symplectic rigidity into geometric analysis.

label: Roadmap
notes: We close the introduction with the map of the book. From the form and Hamiltonian flow we pass through Darboux's local model to global invariants: capacities, fixed-point theorems, and the J-holomorphic curve machinery. Keep the local-flexible versus global-rigid contrast in mind; it recurs on nearly every later page.
